name: Memorystore
oneLiner: Managed in-memory Redis/Memcached for microsecond caching on GCP.
whatItIs: Memorystore is Google Cloud's managed in-memory data store, offering Redis (and Valkey) and Memcached. It keeps hot data in RAM for microsecond reads, so it's the speed layer that sits in front of slower databases: the app checks Memorystore first and only queries Cloud SQL/Bigtable on a miss, cutting latency and load. Redis on Memorystore also backs sessions, rate limiters, leaderboards and pub/sub. Like all caches, it's an accelerator holding a copy of hot data — not the durable system of record.

inPractice.narrative: A busy service reads product data on every request. Rather than hit Cloud SQL each time, it caches results in Memorystore (Redis): the first read fills the cache, later reads return in microseconds, and the database sees only a fraction of the load. Writes update Cloud SQL and invalidate the cached key. Memorystore sits between the app and the database as a fast copy of hot data, not the source of truth.

coreConcepts.detail: Data in RAM gives sub-millisecond access, far faster than disk-backed databases — but memory is finite and volatile by default.
Redis/Valkey brings rich data structures, replication, persistence and pub/sub; Memcached is a simpler pure cache. Most new workloads choose Redis/Valkey.
App reads cache, loads from the database on a miss and populates the cache, invalidating on writes; TTLs bound staleness.
Standard tier adds a replica with automatic failover for HA; read replicas and clustering scale reads/capacity depending on the offering.
Eviction policies (e.g. LRU) and TTLs manage a full cache and control staleness vs hit rate.
Instances run inside your VPC for private, low-latency access from GCP compute — no public exposure by default.

whenToUse: Caching hot data to reduce database load and latency (cache-aside).
Session stores, rate limiting, counters and leaderboards.
Sub-millisecond reads a disk-backed database can't deliver.
Redis pub/sub or lightweight coordination alongside caching.
Absorbing read spikes in front of Cloud SQL/Bigtable.
whenNotToUse: As the durable system of record — it's volatile, finite memory.
Datasets too large to hold economically in RAM.
Analytical queries and joins — use BigQuery.
Data that cannot tolerate loss without careful persistence design.

keyFacts.label: HA
keyFacts.value: Standard tier replica with automatic failover.

keyFacts.label: Durability
keyFacts.value: Volatile by default; Redis persistence optional.

keyFacts.label: Billing
keyFacts.value: Per GB-hour of provisioned capacity by tier.

pricingShape: Memorystore bills by provisioned capacity — GB-hours of memory by service tier — running continuously, plus the standby replica on the HA (Standard) tier. Cost therefore tracks how much RAM you keep online, so sizing to your hot working set rather than your whole dataset is the main lever, along with a good eviction/TTL policy to keep hit rates high. There's no per-request charge on the classic instances; you pay for capacity. Committed-use discounts help steady workloads.
gotchas: It's a cache, not a database — keep the durable copy in Cloud SQL/Bigtable/etc.
Cache invalidation is hard; missed invalidations serve stale data.
Under-provisioned memory plus eviction kills the hit rate and the benefit.
A cold cache after failover briefly stampedes the backing database — plan warm-up.
Persistence/replication must be chosen deliberately if you need any durability.
